extracted.intended_audience: legal scholars, patent practitioners, policymakers, patent examiners, and students interested in AI and intellectual property law
extracted.subtask_description: Comparative doctrinal analysis of the criteria and legal standards for patenting inventions produced by or with the assistance of artificial intelligence, including inventorship, patentability requirements, and recommended policy reforms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty
rubrics_metrics.description: The invention must be new, meaning it should not form part of the prior art—i.e., it should not have been publicly disclosed before the filing date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applied to AI-generated outputs, novelty assessment must account for AI systems' reliance on pre-existing data sets and machine learning models, which can blur the delineation between computational output and creative inventiveness. Examiners must determine whether AI-derived results were already publicly disclosed via training data or other prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventive Step / Non-Obviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: The invention should involve an inventive step that would not be obvious to a person having ordinary skill in the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: AI challenges the non-obviousness inquiry because systems can generate solutions in ways opaque to their creators; examiners must assess whether the AI output reflects a non-obvious contribution beyond what PHOSITA would derive. The dissertation notes concerns about how to fairly and consistently evaluate AI-generated inventions for non-obviousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Industrial Applicability / Utility
rubrics_metrics.description: The invention must be capable of industrial application or provide a specific, substantial, and credible utility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Traditional formulation applies to AI-generated inventions as well—claims should demonstrate real-world applicability. The work reiterates the standard wording (industrial applicability/utility) used across jurisdictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentable Subject Matter
rubrics_metrics.description: The invention must fall within the domain of patentable subject matter, which varies by jurisdiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: AI-related inventions raise questions about whether outputs (especially pure software, algorithms, or machine-generated works) are within patent-eligible subject matter in particular jurisdictions; the paper emphasizes variation across the United States, EU, UK, India, China, Japan, and others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventorship (Conception as Touchstone)
rubrics_metrics.description: Inventorship is traditionally tied to human conception; 'conception is the touchstone of inventorship,' which must involve a mental act performed by a human being.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many legal systems (e.g., under U.S. law and EPC) require a natural person as inventor. The dissertation highlights cases (e.g., University of Utah v. Max-Planck; DABUS filings) where applications naming an AI as inventor were rejected on the grounds that inventorship is limited to natural persons. Improper designation of inventors can lead to invalidation of patents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to Designate an Inventor in Application
rubrics_metrics.description: Procedural requirement in some regimes (e.g., EPC) to designate the inventor in the application process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because many patent offices require inventor designation and assume a human inventor, attempts to list AI systems (such as DABUS) have been rejected; procedural rules thus interact with substantive inventorship doctrines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sufficiency of Disclosure / Enablement / Written Description
rubrics_metrics.description: In exchange for exclusive rights, inventors must disclose their inventions in sufficient detail so that others skilled in the art can replicate them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The dissertation stresses the classic enablement/written description requirement and implies examination challenges where AI-generated inventions are opaque—examiners and applicants must ensure the specification reveals sufficient technical information to allow replication by a skilled person.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determination of Ownership / Attribution
rubrics_metrics.description: Who legally owns the patent rights: the inventor/author by default, but ownership may be assigned or arise via doctrines like work-for-hire or co-authorship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In the AI context, ownership may be attributed to the developer, owner, or end-user of the AI; the dissertation discusses practical approaches (work-for-hire, co-authorship) and the difficulties because AI lacks legal personhood. Choice of attribution has implications for licensing, enforcement, and successors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal Personhood of AI and Inventorship Recognition
rubrics_metrics.description: The question whether a machine or algorithm can be regarded as an 'inventor' under existing legal frameworks (AI lacks legal personality).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Options considered include (a) reinterpreting existing definitions to include AI-assisted contributions; (b) recognizing developers/owners as proxy inventors; (c) creating sui generis rights for machine-generated inventions; or (d) granting AI legal personhood—each carries complex implications for ownership, liability, and international harmonization. The paper cites South Africa's DABUS grant as an outlier.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment of Prior Art and Training Data Issues
rubrics_metrics.description: AI systems are often trained on vast datasets; delineating between training-data-derived content and genuinely novel inventive contribution is necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The dissertation highlights that examiners must consider whether an AI's output is effectively a recombination of prior art present in training data and whether that precludes novelty or inventive step. The opacity of training processes complicates this assessment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opacity / Explainability Problem
rubrics_metrics.description: Many AI systems operate in ways that are opaque even to their creators, making it difficult to assess how an invention was derived.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This 'black-box' character raises practical difficulties for patent examiners when evaluating inventive contribution and for meeting disclosure/enablement requirements; it may necessitate new examination practices or documentary evidence showing human direction or contribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risk of Non-Disclosure and Trade Secret Reliance
rubrics_metrics.description: If innovators are unsure whether AI-generated creations are eligible for patent protection, they may opt for trade secrets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper warns this could reduce public availability of knowledge and stifle collaborative progress. Policy design should seek to avoid perverse incentives that push innovators away from patent disclosure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improper Inventorship Consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: Improper designation of inventors can lead to the invalidation of patents and disputes over ownership.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The dissertation emphasizes legal consequences—ownership disputes, invalidation, and impacts on employers, employees, and institutions—thus procedural accuracy in naming inventors remains critical even in AI contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparative Jurisdictional Treatment
rubrics_metrics.description: Different jurisdictions present distinct approaches to defining inventorship, assigning legal rights, and interpreting patentability in the AI context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The work compares the US, EU, UK, India, China, Japan, South Africa and others to highlight divergence and areas for potential harmonization. Practitioners must account for jurisdiction-specific rules (e.g., statutory wording, office guidelines like EPO Guidelines G‑II 3.1, and case law such as DABUS decisions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Philosophical and Ethical Implications of Non-Human Inventorship
rubrics_metrics.description: Consideration of ethical, jurisprudential, and policy questions raised by granting inventorship or patent rights to non-human entities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beyond doctrinal mechanics, the paper urges analysis of whether expanding inventorship aligns with foundational IP principles and what social/legal consequences (moral rights, accountability) such a shift entails.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy Reform Options and Criteria for Evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: Potential reforms include reinterpreting inventorship to include AI-assisted contributions, introducing sui generis rights for machine-generated inventions, recognizing developers/owners as proxy inventors, and fostering international harmonization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The dissertation evaluates these options against goals such as encouraging innovation, ensuring legal certainty, preserving core patent principles (novelty, non-obviousness, disclosure), and practicality of enforcement. Each reform's trade-offs (e.g., ownership clarity vs. moral/legal accountability) are discussed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical Evidence Standards to Establish Human Contribution
rubrics_metrics.description: Standards and forms of proof required to demonstrate human conception or meaningful human contribution when AI is involved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although not exhaustively prescribed, the dissertation underscores the need for documentary evidence, records of human direction, or design choices to establish inventorship—important where AI involvement is substantial or autonomous (illustrated by DABUS disputes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Interaction with Copyright Doctrines (Authorship, Work-for-Hire, Co-authorship)
rubrics_metrics.description: In the copyright context, the author is presumed to be the first copyright owner; AI complicates authorship but doctrines like work-for-hire and co-authorship may attribute ownership to humans or organizations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While primarily about copyright, these doctrines provide practical analogues for attributing ownership of AI-generated outputs in IP law more generally; the dissertation discusses moral rights, economic rights, and statutory indicators of human authorship (e.g., lifespan, heirs).

rubrics_metrics.name: Enforcement, Liability and Practical Ownership Issues
rubrics_metrics.description: Legal accountability, enforcement practicality, and liability considerations underlying any decision about inventorship and ownership.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The dissertation notes that recognizing a non-human inventor raises enforcement and liability problems (who sues/who is sued), which are reasons many jurisdictions resist non-human inventorship. These practicalities weigh heavily in policy design.
